title: Statics
note: A body in static equilibrium has zero net force and zero net moment: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0. Start every problem with a free-body diagram that isolates the body and shows all external forces, including support reactions. In 2D that gives three equations, so you can solve for three unknowns.

read.title: Drawing the forces first
text: Statics rests on one idea: a body that is not accelerating has no net force and no net moment acting on it. Every bridge, shelf, crane, and ladder that stays put obeys ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.

The tool that turns this idea into answers is the free-body diagram. You draw the body alone, cut free from everything around it, then replace each support and contact with the forces it exerts. A pin can push in any direction, so it becomes two force components. A roller can only push perpendicular to its surface, so it becomes one. A fixed wall can push and also twist, so it adds a moment. Weight acts at the center of gravity, and a spread-out load can be replaced by its total placed at its centroid.

In two dimensions this gives three equations: forces in x, forces in y, and moments about any point. Choosing that point where unknown forces meet removes them from the moment equation and often solves the problem in one line. If there are more unknowns than equations, the structure is statically indeterminate, and you need its deformations to find the forces.
Trusses apply the same rules joint by joint. Because their members are pinned at the ends, each carries pure tension or compression.
